processing: Lightly oxidised and rolled into semi-balls, as is typical of Taiwanese high-mountain oolong. Most is left unroasted; a low roast shifts it towards grain, and heavy-roasted versions also exist.
harvest_season: Sold as spring and winter harvests, both listed by name by Taiwanese tea sellers.
appearance_dry: Tight, dark-green semi-rolled balls with little scent of milk until brewed.
appearance_liquor: Clear pale gold with a green tint.
appearance_wet: Whole, soft green leaves that open fully over several steeps.
taste_profile: Smooth and sweet with a gentle natural milkiness and light florals, and little astringency. Unroasted lots lean towards milk candy, lightly roasted ones towards toasted grain.

brewing.notes: Give the rolled leaf a long first steep. A very strong milk smell from the dry leaf is a warning sign, not a feature.

vintage_note: Sold by year and harvest, chiefly the spring and winter pickings of the current year. Unroasted lots are best drunk fresh, usually within a year or so as with other green-style oolongs. Roasted versions are a separate product and keep longer.
description:
This is the Jin Xuan cultivar grown in the Alishan tea area of Chiayi, in southern Taiwan. Jin Xuan is the variety behind most milk oolong, and at Alishan it is the side branch to the main crop of Qing Xin Oolong.

The making follows the usual Taiwanese high-mountain pattern, light oxidation and semi-ball rolling, and the roast decides much of the character. Unroasted tea keeps the milk and flower notes up front, while a low roast pushes them into the background behind grain.

In the cup it is smooth and sweet with hardly any bite. The milkiness is real but quiet, and it shows best in the first few steeps with water near the boil. People tend to under-steep rolled leaf at the start, so allow it time to open.

The main trap is flavouring: some milk oolong on the market is scented. Natural Jin Xuan smells fairly restrained when dry, so a tea that fills the room with custard before it meets water is probably not what you want. Ask for the harvest and the area, since Alishan on a label covers a wide range of gardens.
history:
Jin Xuan was bred at Taiwan's Tea Research and Extension Station from a cross of Ying Zhi Hong Xin and Tainong No. 8, and was named in 1981 as TTES No. 12. It is now the second most widely planted tea cultivar on the island, after Qing Xin Oolong.

The Alishan area spans several Chiayi townships, including Meishan and Zhuqi. When Jin Xuan first went in there is not well documented, and the name is a description of cultivar and place rather than a formally defined style.
